title: Passing Lists to Functions
objective: Recognize that a function receives the same list object it was passed, and use a copy when the original must stay unchanged.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.chapterTitle: Passing a List; Preventing a Function from Modifying a List
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: When you pass a list to a function, the function receives the exact same list object the caller has — not a copy. If the function appends to it, sorts it, or removes items from it, those changes are visible back in the caller too, once the function returns.

This is different from passing a number or a string, where the function only ever works with its own value. Lists (and other mutable objects) are shared, so a function that changes one in place changes it everywhere it's referenced.

When you don't want a function to touch the original list, give it a copy instead: roster[:] or list(roster) both create a brand-new list with the same items, so anything the function does to the copy leaves the original untouched.
explanation.rule: A function that receives a list can modify the caller's original list in place, unless it's given a copy instead.

examples.title: Modifying the Original
examples.code:
def add_topping(toppings, new_topping):
    toppings.append(new_topping)

pizza = ["cheese"]
add_topping(pizza, "pepperoni")
print(pizza)
examples.note: add_topping() appends directly to the same list object pizza refers to, so the caller sees the new topping too.

examples.title: Protecting the Original with a Copy
examples.code:
def preview_topping(toppings, new_topping):
    preview = toppings[:]
    preview.append(new_topping)
    return preview

pizza = ["cheese"]
print(preview_topping(pizza, "olives"))
print(pizza)
examples.note: toppings[:] makes a separate copy, so appending to preview never touches the original pizza list.

checks.question: add_scores(scores) appends a number to the list it receives. After calling add_scores(my_scores), what happens to my_scores?
options: my_scores gains the new number too, since the function shares the same list.
A copy of my_scores is created automatically.

feedback.correct: Correct — the function receives the same list object, so appending inside it changes my_scores as well.
feedback.incorrect: A list passed to a function is shared, not copied, so changes made inside the function are visible outside it too.

assignment.title: Recruit Roster
assignment.brief: Write enlist(roster, name), which appends name directly to the given roster list (modifying it in place, no return needed). Then write preview_enlist(roster, name), which returns a brand-new list with name added, without changing the original roster at all.
requirements: Define enlist(roster, name) that appends name to roster in place.
Define preview_enlist(roster, name) that builds a copy of roster (e.g. roster[:]), appends name to the copy, and returns the copy.
preview_enlist must not modify the original roster list.
assignment.testHarness:
# ---- Code Forge validation ----
import io, contextlib
_cf_buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(_cf_buf):
    roster = ["Nyx", "Bram"]
    enlist(roster, "Fen")
    print(roster)
    preview = preview_enlist(roster, "Ghost")
    print(preview)
    print(roster)
_cf_result = _cf_buf.getvalue()
print("__CF_TEST_OUTPUT__")
print(repr(_cf_result))
assignment.outputCheckLabel: enlist() mutates roster in place; preview_enlist() leaves roster unchanged

hints: enlist() just needs one line: roster.append(name).
preview_enlist() should not touch roster directly — start by copying it with roster[:].
Append name to the copy, not to roster, then return the copy.
After both calls, roster should show Fen (from enlist) but never Ghost (which only exists in the returned preview).
